title: First Blood
review: Honestly this movie does so much, the narrative being a narrative and representation for the Vietnam war, a deeper dive into the victims of the war subtextually represent by rambo, explores how these emotions are rationalized by different people, god it does so much. A deconstruction of the appropriated and commodified version of the American mythology in the story of a man just trying to live his life while the systems in place try to pressure him out. Rambo represented so many of us as minorities, disproportionately affected by a system not made for us, the ending really shows this. Him crying about the life he was lived, the privilege and self he once had, all being lost and know all his wants have slowly eroded away to the point where he just wants a hug, and it takes an entire community to be set on fire so it can be given to him. We are conditioned and the moment we aren't useful, all of who we were conditioned to be is gone as well.

title: Stalker
review:
It reminded of me when I was a kid, I used to play in the park with my friends, and at some point we would reach the edge of the playground where the woods were. We all had stories to tell about it, and yet none of us had entered inside. At some point I explored the woods on my own and told them everything I saw in there, including the fantasy I made up. I had nothing to compare it to at the time so the ponds became oceans, the streams became rivers, everything was grand to me because it was the grandest thing I had seen up to that point. When the other kids joined the walk, some saw the spectacle and got scared of it. Others were more skeptical, walking forward, ignoring the little seeds that stick to your clothes, and having a terrible time afterwards. Because of the emotion we had about the stories we told each other about the woods, we believed the same fantasy and world when we entered it as well. The untrained eye would see a bunch of kids running around through a dirt trail with no adult supervision. no adults directly being there to hold there hand through it. I think that's what made it all special was because there was no one there to tell us how to feel about it, we did that on our own, the lack of expectations is what made it special. And yeah That's kinda what this movie reminds me about type shit
I need to rewatch it, I really wished there was a English dub, very long movie, had no climax, and it's a unstructured narrative. It feels like a supplemental peice/a part to a grander world, it's makes me very curious of tarkovsky's other work and himself.

title: Backrooms
review:
I was talking to my friend about this, I really love the parallel it creates between the macro and micro stories and how they are stringed together. Seeing Renate story in the movie, a therapist who used her childhood trauma to find closure and commercial success ("the book she made about windows and how she was trying to escape through the window while she was a kid and was never able to")((Honestly a super interesting idea too, the character selling a form of freedom to others even though she never got it herself, presenting this moral question about white lies as a form of help)) this then being imparted into the macro story of the backrooms, a place that exists as a memory's memory of a place, recursive and abstracted to the idea it once was and now is. Her memory of her past and as well as Chiwetel, they are still living in those days, they haven't escaped the memory they are stuck in, and as the backroom does to itself, they do the same, existing in their own memory, abstracting and re-living a place that never existed as their past has now become a memory, they do too because they are still living in it. It's a little hard to describe with words, which is what the movie also understands (as you can tell with the ending) so they choose for the audience to experience it rather than try to explain it, which I think is a reasonable direction to go in. Also the monologue about our mind creating mental barriers to protect itself from trauma/self-reflection, and how the backrooms does that to protect itself from the abstractions it created, holllyyyy tufff bro thats so cool, they should have totally explored that idea more. That's honestly my only gripe about this movie, it put so many ideas in single movie that, while are expressed fully, aren't given enough time to be digested. I think this really arises at the end of the movie, where it kinda stops at the peak of its influence rather than pushing the audience to new ideas/fully exploring them because it reached it's run time. Makes me wish that Kane gets more opportunities to tell more stories, because if this is just the start, I can't wait to see the next. Also also, for the amount of ideas that this movie has in it, feels a lot more like a nerd (I mean that affectionately) who's info-dumping his favorite custom DND campaign he made that his friends like than it feels like a director who created a modern-classic. The first definitely has it's own charm attached to it, and a lot of directors kinda start out like that (the first ex that came to my head was Quentin Tarantino) so I wonder what direction Kane will head in, if given the opportunity. 

Pretty swag movie though for sure type shit

title: They Cloned Tyrone
review: It's a interesting perspective on created systemic issues because it shows that if you did create a perfect system to control people in mass, with a competent governing body able to clone and create at will, it still wouldn't work because control functions as a recursive tool. You can only control what you have, you can't control what you don't. If you use control to create world peace, as they do in this movie, you would have to make everyone either be brainwashed, indoctrinated, and/or apart of the system to make that peace, and at that point is it peace or is it ideology that is destroying itself to exist? Pretty alright, got a lot of ideas working in the lines, and is pretty funny at times. I liked it, might rewatch it!

title: The Holdovers
review: Helped me realize that while all grief calluses into different forms from different stories, to have grief never comes from a bad place. We all need grief to a certain extent because it leads us to find closure for ourselves. Grief and closure can lead us to many things, but  to find a path you like is to have people who went through it too with you. A limitation is can heal you, and a limitation can hold onto you if you have no control over the limits you've set. Grief is a very beautiful thing that needs to be cherished because you only get it a few times in your life. There's only so many people that materialize the care you set for them, to reciprocate balance onto you, and for that relationship to experience grief, is the furthest exploration bounded by the edges of an relationship. We often never get to be that far into a person's life, until it starts become normalized.  A person dies every second but that doesn't mean it happens often. When a star dies, that's only what we call it by. It changes beings, into supernovas, black-holes, white dwarfs, the only thing that changed is what we remembered it by. And to the being that's now here, they never changed into something they are not, this how they've always been.

title: Lady Bird
review:
This movie was made with a specific audience to accommodate for, and I think it works incredibly well within that audience. It's like the people who rate marvel movies 5 stars for comic accuracy, and they enjoy every little detail the writers left for them in the movie. The movie stands more as a reference rather than a actual point. It just states similarities in emotional relationships that we have within our love and our past. This movie lets you feel emotionally fulfilled by validating observations you made in your life and referencing them. That isn't a critique to the movie, that's what makes it good in the first place. If you don't see yourself as the characters, you just wouldn't get the same enjoyment out of the movie, making it feel simple; but not shallow. A marvel movie can well written for fans, but a regular fan will only observe the fact its well written; not experience it. 

I hope that makes sense please do correct me if I'm wrong.

title: Saturday Night Fever
review: Literally everything aged terribly and this movie definitely needed at least 4 more re writes before it could actually be anything related to "good". That's not to say it isn't foundational. Everything fundamental to this movie is sound. But there are so many themes being portrayed, none of them should work - and so they add up to a coagulated piece. Everything is so half baked outside of the dancing and club, the only characters I really cared about were the woman, mostly because of how fucked up everyone was treating them. This movie tried to be the outsiders for disco but the material is just so conceptually bad. None of the ideas work, and they never dive into anything they want to talk about. I really think there could have been good story here with broken characters, but it all ends up as liquid goop for a under-paid janitor to mop up un-properly so there's just a nasty stain left the next day.
